drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: An operations lead asks Claude to compare three vendor proposals
drills.scenario: Vendor comparison, ten of twelve rows
drills.stem: Claude compares three vendor proposals against a 12-point requirements list and recommends Vendor B for the procurement committee. The table has 10 rows. What is the best next action?

options.A: Send it, since Claude most likely dropped the two requirements that did not separate the vendors
options.B: Ask Claude to score the two missing requirements, quoting each proposal, then check those rows and whether the recommendation holds
options.C: Rerun the whole comparison on the most capable model
options.D: Send it with a note telling the committee the comparison may be incomplete

drills.why: Check the output against the brief and fill the gap. D is a disclosure dressed as a fix; A trusts the model; C overspends and still needs checking.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A sales lead asks Claude to turn her call notes
drills.answer_line: SAM: C. Neither detail traces to the source
drills.scenario: Case study with an untraceable quote
drills.stem: A draft customer case study for the website includes a quote from the customer's finance director and a 40% cut in onboarding time. The call notes contain neither. What should the sales lead do?

options.A: Keep both, since Claude probably inferred them from the context of the call
options.B: Ask Claude whether the quote is accurate, and keep it if Claude says yes
options.C: Remove the quote and figure unless the customer confirms them, and check every other specific against the notes
options.D: Soften the figure to "around 40%" and keep the quote

drills.why: Neither detail traces to the source, so both are invented until confirmed. One invented specific is a reason to check the rest.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A consultant is using Claude to summarise
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. A limits Claude to the source
drills.stem: Choose two. A consultant summarises a 60-page regulatory consultation for a client deck and wants to reduce the risk of invented details. Which two steps help most?

options.A: Tell Claude to use only the uploaded document and say plainly when it does not cover a point
options.B: Ask Claude to quote the passage supporting each key claim, then check those quotes against the document
options.C: Ask Claude for a confidence percentage per claim and drop any under 80
options.D: Ask for a more authoritative tone so the client trusts it
options.E: Add "be accurate" in capitals to the prompt

drills.why: A limits Claude to the source and exposes gaps; B makes every claim checkable. Self-rated confidence is more generated text, not a check.

drills.label: Dropdown
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. This is a dropdown item
drills.prompt: For each, human review before use, or self-check is enough? 1. Ten name ideas for a team offsite. 2. Plain-language summary of a patient's discharge instructions, for the patient. 3. Internal analysis that will set next year's list prices. 4. Claude's rewording of a paragraph in your own internal newsletter.
drills.answer: 1 Self-check. 2 Human review (clinician). 3 Human review: internal, but it sets prices for every customer. 4 Self-check that the meaning is unchanged.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: The other half is comparing drafts.
drills.answer_line: SAM: But tone is the cheap part to fix
drills.scenario: Two drafts of an office-move announcement
drills.stem: Staff raised four questions about an office move: date, parking, desk booking, who to contact. Draft one is warm and polished and answers two. Draft two is plainer and answers all four. What should the communications manager do?

options.A: Send draft one, because tone matters most for staff news
options.B: Ask Claude which draft is better and send that one
options.C: Take draft two, since it meets the brief, and edit its tone for the audience
options.D: Send both and let staff use whichever they prefer

drills.why: Tone is cheap to fix; completeness is expensive. Start from the draft that meets the brief. B hands the judgement back with no criteria.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. An H R partner needs a two-page onboarding guide
drills.stem: An HR partner needs a two-page onboarding guide. She will revise it with Claude over several rounds this week, then share it with hiring managers. Which output suits the task best?

options.A: An inline reply, copied into a document after each round
options.B: An artifact, so the guide stands on its own beside the conversation and can be revised and shared
options.C: The guide as structured data with one field per section
options.D: A series of short messages, one per section

drills.why: Substantial, self-contained, revised over rounds, then shared: the artifact test. Structured data suits data that feeds a tool, not prose.

drills.question_line: SAM: Recall first. Pause and name the five segments
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Accuracy, hallucinations and bias: check the specifics.
drills.prompt: Name the five segments, and the check that goes with each.
drills.answer: Accuracy, hallucinations and bias: check the specifics. Fact-checking: the source, with quotes. Human review: stakes and audience. Editing: meet the brief, keep the facts. Formats: inline, artifact, structured data.

In this episode: Judge accuracy, and what the draft left out
Spot invented figures, contradictions and slanted framing
Pick the checking technique that catches the error
Decide when a person must review
Adapt and compare drafts for the reader
Choose inline, artifact or structured data
Cold open: the vendor comparison: Six objectives: accuracy and completeness, hallucinations and bias, fact-checking
...human review, editing for the audience, output formats
Right answer: the diligent, proportionate step
Distractors: trust confidence, overspend, ask the model to promise, give up, polish
Accuracy, hallucinations and bias: Accuracy: is it true? Completeness: is it all there?
A missing item leaves no trace on the page
Hallucination: plausible content grounded in nothing
Fluency and confidence say nothing about accuracy
Inconsistency: the draft contradicts itself or its source
Bias: one-sided framing, or a prompt that leaks the answer
Fact-checking techniques: Other techniques make that check faster or narrower
Same request twice: disagreement marks a fact to check
A citation is a place to check, not a check
When a human must review: Raise the bar for stakes, audience, reversibility, specialist content
Stem words: customer, patient, regulator, board, contract, published
Brainstorm, first pass, draft for myself: self-check
The reviewer must be able to tell if it is wrong
Editing for the audience: Customer: plain words, no internal jargon
A rewrite can change facts while it changes tone
Formats: inline, artifact, structured da: Three formats: inline, artifact, structured data
Artifact for everything? A two-line answer gains nothing
Structured data: rows to compare, sort or feed a tool
Name the columns and keep them the same each time
Curate: reader's need first, group, drop duplicates
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: B, cover the two missing rows with quoted evidence and recheck
D: a disclosure dressed as a fix
A: trusts the model's reasons for dropping rows
C: a bigger model, and the table still needs checking
Five to remember: Confidence is not accuracy: check specifics against the source
Completeness: check against the brief, never by rereading
Source first; limit to documents, allow "I don't know", quote per claim
Review scales with stakes, audience, reversibility, specialism
Inline, artifact or structured data; adapting keeps facts and caveats
Recap: the exam tells: Precise figure or quote not in the source → invented until confirmed
Output covers less than asked → check against the brief, fill the gap
Option asks Claude how confident it is → distractor
Output includes citations, important reader → still open the sources
Customer, patient, regulator, board → review by someone qualified
Polish versus completeness → complete draft, then edit tone
Rewrite softens a caveat → the rewrite is wrong
Quick → inline; stand-alone and shared → artifact; rows → structured data
